articles.title: Wallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profit
articles.summary: Animation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s content. Don’t break out the celebratory Wensleydale just yet. Aardman, the British animation studio behind the cheese-loving inventor Wallace and his beloved dog Gromit, has fallen short of a target to get back…
body: The employee-owned business was aiming to record a small profit in 2025 after two years of consecutive losses but was hit by production delays and a “challenging market” in children’s content.
So although its revenues jumped 8% to £20.4m last year, it was in the red to the tune of £1.1m, albeit an improvement on the previous year’s £4.1m loss.
Aardman, which also produces the popular Shaun the Sheep series, said the timing of some “significant” deals and weaker income in some parts of the business had hurt its bottom line.

It will be hoping for a boost from new projects, such as a recently opened exhibition at Lightroom in London that explores its 54-year history, as well as a third Shaun the Sheep film, which was released last month.

articles.title: By Design review – Juliette Lewis turns into a chair in hypnotic Lynchian drama
articles.summary: A musician becomes obsessed with the haunted seat, but the potentially hilarious premise sleepwalks its way to an unsatisfying conclusion. The indie indulgences of US film-maker Amanda Kramer – which often contain big names making small appearances – are such a puzzle; sometimes they work…
body: By Design is an all but unbearable absurdist drama. The actors deliver halting dialogue as if in a hypnotic trance, paralysed by the film’s heavy conceit: Juliette Lewis plays a depressed single woman who turns into a chair. The scene seems set for some entertaining hijinks with visual effects, in which Lewis and the chair merge. But no – not really. What in fact happens is that Lewis’s own body is supposedly robbed of its animating identity or spirit, which migrates into the chair while she becomes catatonic, a body flopped down on the bed. The chair itself doesn’t look or behave in any way differently.

Mamoudou Athie, doing his considerable best, plays a musician whose girlfriend buys him this haunted chair as a kind of guilt offering for walking out on him, and he becomes obsessed with it – although the comic or erotic potential of this transgressive idea is entirely neglected. The chair’s designer (a gamey cameo for the now late Udo Kier ) declares there is something strange about it but he can’t decide what it is. And so the film sleepwalks its way to a conclusion as unsatisfying as everything that has gone before. Someone somewhere should give Lewis a decent role.

articles.title: ‘To succeed meant to leave’: inside the jolting film about Brummie estate kids knocked flying by demolition
articles.summary: The novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals all.
body: A s a kid in 90s Birmingham, Keiran Goddard would gather with his friends to watch the tower blocks coming down. That’s what passed for entertainment back then. Controlled explosions, collapsing buildings. The demolition of Shard End’s postwar council estates marked the end of one story and the start of another. It was a dust-blown display of regeneration and progress. The housing that replaced it would be an improvement. The people of east Birmingham would move on to better lives.

Goddard, specifically, moved on to study English at Oxford University. He now lives in London and writes books for a living. Physically, he has left his home town far behind. Emotionally and spiritually, not so much. “So I feel quite splintered,” he says. “I’m not sure anyone ever really leaves the world they grew up in.”

Goddard’s Birmingham-set second novel has just been made into a film. Enda Walsh wrote the script; Clio Barnard called the shots. Set in and around Shard End, I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is a jolting, stirring ensemble drama in which a tower block’s demolition serves as a kind of societal big bang, spinning five childhood friends into a fraught adulthood.

articles.title: YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom
articles.summary: A new virtuous circle is emerging for media and entertainment giants that promises to harness the advantages of disparate platforms, digital and linear, powered by the connective tissue of YouTube.
body: Evan Shapiro, the respected industry analyst who is often billed as a “media cartographer,” gave a well-attended presentation on Wednesday morning that drew together threads probed in various tracks of the conference. Shapiro’s session offered sobering stats about the changing nature of viewing audiences. The older contingent of media and entertainment leaders have to come to grips with the fact that the world’s population is getting younger. That means they need to cater to consumers who have come of age with technology in their pockets and a very different worldview on how, when and why they consume media in across different mediums and platforms.
At the same time, Shapiro pointed to hope on the horizon for legacy media outlets.

“We believed television would be replaced by streaming 1 for 1 — that didn’t happen,” he said. Streaming and social video have augmented viewing time and even more important, they help deepen fan connection to their favorite shows. Shapiro emphasized more than once that media giants courting audiences need to think in terms of generations and affinity groups, not the age and gender demos of yore.
points: A new virtuous circle is emerging for media and entertainment giants that promises to harness the advantages of disparate platforms, digital and linear, powered by the connective tissue of YouTube.

articles.title: Iranian Filmmaker Majid Majidi Denounces U.S. War as ‘Midday Meal’ Emerges as Busan Fest Standout
articles.summary: The Oscar-nominated director nearly skipped Asia's leading film festival, but ultimately decided to attend so that he could speak out about the war’s toll on ordinary Iranians.
body: Iranian director Majid Majidi says he originally planned to decline the Busan International Film Festival ’s invitation to travel to South Korea to premiere his latest feature, Midday Meal. A gripping and heartfelt humanist parable filmed with the command of an established master, the film has since emerged as one of the standouts of the festival’s 2026 competition, with many festivalgoers calling it a front-runner for the top prize.

The director declined to describe how he made the journey from Tehran to South Korea. His visit came amid a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, reimposed in July, and sweeping September sanctions targeting Iranian aviation. Once in Busan, though, he was forceful in denouncing the civilian deaths and everyday hardships caused by the U.S. campaign against his country.

articles.title: ‘South Park’ Spoofs Clavicular, Looksmaxxing and Sephora in a Peak-Season Episode
articles.summary: Ike enters an aura battle, Stan gets lost in the Backrooms and Randy gets a face-lift.
body: The latest South Park continues the Comedy Central animated series’ return to form after its heavily political 2025 run, this time with a plot built around South Park Elementary’s newest trend: aura battles. The 22-minutes of sharp satire also spoof the beauty retailer Sephora, the hit horror film Backrooms and the looksmaxxing trend, while including several callbacks for longtime fans.

Meanwhile, Sephora has the town’s pre-teen girls in a tizzy. The store is packed when Stan and Wendy arrive, and he quickly loses her in a crowd of screaming kids at the garish makeup counter, where employees slop cream on the girls’ faces and ask the question that gives the episode its title. It’s crude, and it feels inorganic to the scene, but damn, it made me laugh, even when the gag returned later for a second round.

articles.title: At the Brooklyn novelty shop in 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
articles.summary: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.
body: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).
